# Symmetric fields and their constraints {#sec-csdr-symmetric-fields}

Coset space dimensional reduction (CSDR) starts from a gauge theory on a product $M_4 \times S/R$ of spacetime with a
coset space, and keeps not the fields that are independent of the internal coordinates but those that are
*symmetric*: invariant under the isometries of the coset up to a gauge transformation. Because the action of the
isometry group on such fields is a gauge transformation, the Lagrangian evaluated on them is the same at every
internal point, and integrating over the coset gives an honest four-dimensional theory whose solutions are solutions
of the higher-dimensional one. The price is a set of algebraic constraints on the fields, which depend on how the
isotropy group $R$ of the coset is embedded in the gauge group $G$; their solution decides which gauge fields and which
scalars survive in four dimensions. This chapter has two sections. Symmetric fields and the CSDR constraints defines
symmetric gauge fields, splits them into a four-dimensional gauge field and internal scalars, states the constraints
those satisfy and the representation-theoretic rules that solve them, and checks the matching of charges for the running
example. The embedding of $U(1)$ in $SU(3)$ fixes that example: the sphere $S^2 = SO(3)/SO(2) \cong SU(2)/U(1)$, the
gauge group $SU(3)$, and the isotropy $U(1)$ embedded along the hypercharge direction $\lambda_8$; it computes the
eigenspaces of the embedded generator and identifies the four-dimensional gauge group $SU(2) \times U(1)$. The next
chapter solves the constraints and derives the Higgs potential. Every statement is followed by three examples and
three exercises with folded solutions, and the chapter ends with three integrative exercises.

The construction goes back to Forgács and Manton [@forgacs1980] and to Harnad, Shnider and Vinet [@harnad1980], who
stated the invariance conditions for gauge fields under a group acting on a principal bundle. It was soon used for
model building: Chapline and Manton gave the geometric meaning of the resulting Higgs potentials [@Chapline:1980mr],
and unified models broken towards the standard model [@Bais:1985yd], dynamical symmetry breaking [@Forgacs:1984zx] and
the reduction of ten-dimensional $E_8$ gauge theory over coset spaces [@Lust:1985be] followed. The reviews
@kapetanakis1992 and @manolakos2016 and the monograph @kubyshin1989 cover the subject in depth.

## Symmetric fields and the CSDR constraints {#sec-csdr-constraints}

Coset space dimensional reduction keeps, instead of the fields independent of the internal coordinates, the
fields that are *symmetric*: invariant under the isometries of the coset up to a gauge transformation. The
Lagrangian evaluated on such fields does not depend on the internal point, so it is an honest four-dimensional
Lagrangian, and the consistency problem of @sec-nonabelian-reduction disappears for the fields kept. This section
defines symmetric gauge fields, derives the constraints they satisfy and the rules that solve them, following
@manolakos2016 [Sec. 2, eqs. 2-13] and @kubyshin2003 [Secs. 2-3], before the running example of Part V, $SU(3)$ over
$S^2 = SU(2)/U(1)$, is worked out in the rest of this chapter and the next. It has four subsections: symmetric gauge
fields, the constraints on the reduced fields, the counting rules, and the matching of charges for the
running example.

### Symmetric gauge fields

A gauge field on a space with symmetries can be asked to be invariant, but for a gauge field invariance is too strong a
requirement: two potentials that differ by a gauge transformation describe the same physics. The definition below asks
only that each isometry act on the field as some gauge transformation, which is the right notion of symmetry for a
gauge theory.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-symmetric-gauge-field}
#### Symmetric gauge field

Let $S$ act on $M_4 \times S/R$ by its left action on the coset (@def-coset-space), with Killing vectors $\xi_A$,
$A = 1, \dots, \dim S$. A gauge field $\hat A$ with gauge group $G$ on $M_4 \times S/R$ is **symmetric** if every
$S$-transformation of it is a gauge transformation: for each generator there is a $G$-valued function $W_A(y)$
with
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\xi_A}\hat A_\alpha = \partial_\alpha W_A - [W_A, \hat A_\alpha] ,
$$ {#eq-symmetric-field}
the infinitesimal gauge transformation @eq-gauge-transformation with parameter $W_A$ [@manolakos2016, eq. 3;
@kubyshin2003, eq. 17]. Scalars and spinors are symmetric when $\mathcal{L}_{\xi_A}\phi = D(W_A)\phi$ in their
representation [@manolakos2016, eqs. 2 and 4].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest symmetric fields are those for which the compensating gauge transformation is not needed at all. The
first example records this case and explains why it is too restrictive on a sphere.

::: {#exm-symmetric-invariant}
#### Strictly invariant fields

$W_A = 0$: the field is invariant under the isometries, $\mathcal{L}_{\xi_A}\hat A = 0$, which for the circle is the
cylinder condition of @def-cylinder-condition. On a sphere the only strictly invariant fields are trivial, and
the compensating gauge transformations are essential.
:::

The magnetic monopole is the standard example of a field that is symmetric without being invariant. Its potential
cannot be rotation invariant, since no potential of a monopole is globally defined, but each rotation changes it only
by a gradient.

::: {#exm-symmetric-monopole}
#### The monopole

The $U(1)$ potential $A = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ of the Hopf fibration (@def-hopf-connection) is not invariant under
rotations, but rotating it changes it by a gradient: it is a symmetric gauge field with $W_A \neq 0$, the first
example of the construction [@kubyshin2003, eq. 32].
:::

The reason for the definition is what it does to the Lagrangian. The third example shows that a symmetric field has a
Lagrangian density that is the same at every point of the coset, so that integrating over the internal space is
trivial.

::: {#exm-symmetric-lagrangian}
#### The Lagrangian is constant on the coset

Since the $S$-action on a symmetric field is a gauge transformation and the Yang-Mills Lagrangian is gauge
invariant, $\mathcal{L}_{YM}(\hat A)$ at $(x, sy)$ equals its value at $(x, y)$: it is a function on $M_4$ alone, the
reduced Lagrangian [@kubyshin2003, p. 6]. This is the basis of the method and the reason it is consistent for the
fields it keeps.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks that the right-hand side of @eq-symmetric-field really is an infinitesimal gauge
transformation, and computes the Lie derivative of a one-form that appears on its left-hand side. Both formulas are
used in every later computation with symmetric fields.

::: {#exr-csd-lie-derivative}
#### The two sides of the definition

(a) Show that for a one-form $A = A_\alpha dy^\alpha$ and a vector field $\xi$, $\mathcal{L}_\xi A = d(\iota_\xi A) +
\iota_\xi dA$ has components $\xi^\beta\partial_\beta A_\alpha + A_\beta\partial_\alpha\xi^\beta$. (b) Show that the gauge
transformation $\hat A \mapsto g^{-1}\hat A g + g^{-1}dg$ with $g = e^{\epsilon W}$ changes $\hat A$ to first order by
$\epsilon(dW - [W, \hat A])$, the right-hand side of @eq-symmetric-field.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) Cartan's formula gives $d(\xi^\beta A_\beta) = (\partial_\alpha\xi^\beta A_\beta + \xi^\beta\partial_\alpha A_\beta)dy^\alpha$ and
$\iota_\xi dA = \xi^\beta(\partial_\beta A_\alpha - \partial_\alpha A_\beta)dy^\alpha$; the terms $\pm\xi^\beta\partial_\alpha A_\beta$ cancel and
leave $\xi^\beta\partial_\beta A_\alpha + A_\beta\partial_\alpha\xi^\beta$. (b) With $g = 1 + \epsilon W + O(\epsilon^2)$, $g^{-1} = 1 - \epsilon W$
and $g^{-1}\hat A g = \hat A + \epsilon(\hat A W - W\hat A)$, $g^{-1}dg = \epsilon\,dW$, so $\delta\hat A = \epsilon(dW - [W, \hat A])$.
The definition therefore says that the infinitesimal motion of the field along $\xi_A$ coincides with an infinitesimal gauge
transformation, with a parameter $W_A$ that may depend on the point.
:::

The second exercise makes the monopole example explicit. For each of the three rotations of the sphere it computes the
Lie derivative of $A = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ and finds the gauge parameter that compensates it.

::: {#exr-csd-monopole-rotation}
#### Rotating the monopole

With the Killing vectors $\xi_1 = -\sin\varphi\,\partial_\theta - \cot\theta\cos\varphi\,\partial_\varphi$, $\xi_2 = \cos\varphi\,\partial_\theta -
\cot\theta\sin\varphi\,\partial_\varphi$, $\xi_3 = \partial_\varphi$ of the round sphere, compute $\mathcal{L}_{\xi_A}A$ for
$A = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ and find functions $W_A$ with $\mathcal{L}_{\xi_A}A = dW_A$. Where are the $W_A$ singular, and why
is that expected?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The rotation about the axis, $\xi_3$, leaves $A$ invariant ($W_3 = 0$); the other two change it by the gradients of
$W_1 = -\cos\varphi/\sin\theta$ and $W_2 = -\sin\varphi/\sin\theta$. For an abelian group the commutator in @eq-symmetric-field
vanishes, so this is exactly the symmetric-field condition. The parameters are singular at the poles, like the
potential itself: $A$ is a potential of a monopole field, and no potential of a monopole is smooth on the whole sphere
(@def-hopf-connection), so the compensating transformations inherit the singularity of the chosen gauge.

{{< sage exr-csd-monopole-rotation >}}
:::

The third exercise proves the statement of @exm-symmetric-lagrangian. It uses only the covariance of the field
strength under gauge transformations and the invariance of the trace.

::: {#exr-csd-lagrangian-constant}
#### Why the Lagrangian is constant

Let $\hat A$ be symmetric. Show that its field strength satisfies $\mathcal{L}_{\xi_A}\hat F = -[W_A, \hat F]$, deduce
$\mathcal{L}_{\xi_A}\operatorname{Tr}(\hat F_{MN}\hat F^{MN}) = 0$ when the $\xi_A$ are Killing vectors, and conclude that the
Lagrangian density is a function on $M_4$ alone.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Lie derivative commutes with $d$, so $\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat F = d(\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat A) + [\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat A, \hat A] +
[\hat A, \mathcal{L}_\xi\hat A]$ (in form notation, $\hat F = d\hat A + \hat A \wedge \hat A$). Substituting
$\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat A = dW - [W, \hat A]$ and using the Jacobi identity, the terms with $dW$ cancel and the rest
combine into $-[W, \hat F]$: the field strength transforms covariantly, as under any gauge transformation
(@def-nonabelian-field-strength). The trace of a commutator with a product vanishes, $\operatorname{Tr}([W, \hat F]\hat F) =
0$, and the metric is preserved by a Killing vector, so the Lie derivative of $\operatorname{Tr}(\hat F_{MN}\hat F^{MN})$
vanishes. A function whose derivative along all the $\xi_A$ vanishes is constant on the orbits of $S$; since $S$ acts
transitively on $S/R$, it depends on $x \in M_4$ only.
:::
::::

### The constraints

With the definition in place, the field on $M_4 \times S/R$ is split into the components along spacetime and along the
coset. The definition below names the four-dimensional fields obtained this way; the conditions they inherit from
@eq-symmetric-field come afterwards.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-csdr-reduced-fields}
#### Reduced fields

Splitting $\hat A_M = (\hat A_\mu, \hat A_a)$ into spacetime and internal components, with $a$ running over the
coset directions of a reductive decomposition $\mathfrak{s} = \mathfrak{r} \oplus \mathfrak{k}$
(@def-reductive-decomposition), the symmetric-field condition @eq-symmetric-field splits into conditions on
$A_\mu(x) = \hat A_\mu$, which becomes the four-dimensional gauge field, and on $\phi_a(x) = \hat A_a$, which become
four-dimensional scalars [@manolakos2016, eq. 10]. The **reduced fields** are $A_\mu$ and $\phi_a$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The precise statement behind this splitting is a classical theorem on invariant connections. The first example quotes
it and identifies its two pieces with the reduced fields.

::: {#exm-reduced-wang}
#### Wang's theorem

Every $S$-invariant connection on $M_4 \times S/R$ is a pair of an unconstrained connection on $M_4$ with gauge
group the centraliser $C_G(\tau(R))$, and a linear map $\phi: \mathfrak{k} \to \mathfrak{g}$ equivariant under $R$
[@kubyshin2003, p. 8]: the reduced fields are exactly $(A_\mu, \phi_a)$ with the constraints below.
:::

In coordinates the symmetric field can be written down explicitly from the Maurer-Cartan form of the coset. The second
example gives this local form, in which the internal components are the scalars contracted with the coset vielbein.

::: {#exm-reduced-local-form}
#### The local form

In a chart with coset representative $s(y)$ and Maurer-Cartan form $s^{-1}ds = \bar\theta_{\mathfrak r} +
\bar\theta_{\mathfrak k}$ (@sec-coset-vielbeins), the symmetric field is $\hat A(x, y) = A(x) + \tau'(\bar\theta_{\mathfrak r}) +
\phi_x(\bar\theta_{\mathfrak k})$ [@kubyshin2003, eq. 23]: the four-dimensional gauge field, the embedded
$R$-connection of @exm-gauge-field-r-connection, and the scalars contracted with the coset vielbein.
:::

The circle is the degenerate case in which the isotropy group is trivial. The third example shows that the method then
reduces to the zero-mode truncation of ordinary Kaluza-Klein theory.

::: {#exm-reduced-circle}
#### The circle

For $S/R = U(1)/\{e\}$ there is no $R$, no constraint, one scalar $\phi_y = \hat A_y$ and the gauge group is all of
$G$: the symmetric fields are the $y$-independent ones, as in Part III.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise counts the reduced fields of the running example before any constraint is imposed. The count is
the starting point against which the effect of the constraints will be measured.

::: {#exr-csd-count-components}
#### Counting before the constraints

For $G = SU(3)$ on $M_4 \times S^2$, how many real four-dimensional fields do $A_\mu$ and $\phi_1, \phi_2$ contain before
the constraints? Anticipating @sec-csdr-embedding and @sec-csdr-solution, how many survive?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$A_\mu$ is an $\mathfrak{su}(3)$-valued vector field, eight real vector fields; $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ are two
$\mathfrak{su}(3)$-valued scalars, sixteen real scalars. After the constraints, $A_\mu$ lies in the four-dimensional
centraliser $\mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(1)$ (four vector fields) and $(\phi_1, \phi_2)$ in a four-dimensional
real solution space, one complex doublet (four real scalars): $8 + 16 = 24$ components reduce to $4 + 4 = 8$.
:::

The second exercise computes the local form of @exm-reduced-local-form for the sphere. It shows how the isotropy
connection and the frame arise from the Maurer-Cartan form of a coset representative.

::: {#exr-csd-local-form-sphere}
#### The Maurer-Cartan form of the sphere

With $Q_a = \sigma_a/2i$ and the coset representative $s(\theta, \varphi) = e^{\varphi Q_3}e^{\theta Q_2}$ of $SU(2)/U(1)$,
compute $s^{-1}ds = \theta^aQ_a$ and identify the $\mathfrak{r}$-component $\theta^3$ and the frame $(\theta^1, \theta^2)$.
Which metric does the frame define, and which potential is $\theta^3$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\theta^1 = -\sin\theta\,d\varphi$, $\theta^2 = d\theta$, $\theta^3 = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$. The frame gives the round metric
$d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$ of the unit sphere, and the isotropy component is the monopole potential of
@exm-symmetric-monopole: the $R$-connection term $\tau(\theta^3 Q_3)$ of the local form is the monopole embedded in $G$
along $\tau(Q_3)$, which is why symmetric fields on the sphere carry a monopole background.

{{< sage exr-csd-local-form-sphere >}}
:::

The third exercise looks at the circle more closely. A constant compensating gauge transformation, allowed by the
definition even when the isotropy group is trivial, produces fields that are not independent of $y$.

::: {#exr-csd-twisted-circle}
#### Twisted fields on the circle

On $M_4 \times S^1$ take $\xi = \partial_y$ and a constant $W \in \mathfrak{g}$. Solve $\partial_y\hat A_\alpha = -[W, \hat A_\alpha]$ (the
condition @eq-symmetric-field with $\partial_\alpha W = 0$) and state the periodicity condition on $W$. How does this relate
to @exm-reduced-circle?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The solution is $\hat A_\alpha(x, y) = e^{-yW}\hat A_\alpha(x, 0)e^{yW}$, a field that rotates in the gauge algebra as one
goes around the circle. It is single-valued if $e^{-2\pi R W}$ (with $y \sim y + 2\pi R$) commutes with all the values of
the field, for instance if it is central in $G$. Such twisted ansätze are allowed by the definition and are again
consistent, but they are gauge equivalent to $y$-independent fields only when $W$ can be removed by a periodic gauge
transformation; the choice $W = 0$ gives the zero modes of @exm-reduced-circle. On a coset with non-trivial $R$ the
compensating transformations are forced, not optional, which is the content of the constraints below.
:::
::::

The splitting of @def-csdr-reduced-fields is not yet useful: the reduced fields still have to satisfy what remains of
@eq-symmetric-field. The definition below lists these conditions, which are purely algebraic once an embedding of
$R$ in $G$ has been chosen.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-csdr-constraints}
#### The CSDR constraints

Choose an embedding $\tau: R \to G$ (a homomorphism, @def-homomorphism). The symmetric-field condition is
equivalent to [@manolakos2016, eq. 12; @kubyshin2003, eq. 22]:

1. $A_\mu$ is independent of $y$ and commutes with $\tau(\mathfrak{r})$: $[\tau(Q_i), A_\mu] = 0$ for the generators
   $Q_i$ of $R$;
2. the scalars are $R$-equivariant, $[\tau(Q_i), \phi_a] = f_{ia}{}^b\phi_b$, where $f_{ia}{}^b$ are the structure
   constants of $[Q_i, Q_a] = f_{ia}{}^bQ_b$ (@eq-coset-structure);
3. the components along $R$ are fixed, $\phi_i = \tau(Q_i)$.

The constraints are algebraic: they are solved once, at a point of the coset.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Each of the three constraints has a direct meaning. The first example reads the first constraint as the choice of the
four-dimensional gauge group.

::: {#exm-constraints-gauge-group}
#### The four-dimensional gauge group

Constraint 1 says that $A_\mu$ takes values in the centraliser $\mathfrak{h} = \{X \in \mathfrak{g} : [\tau(Q_i), X] =
0\}$: the reduced gauge group is $H = C_G(\tau(R))$ [@manolakos2016, p. 3], computed for $SU(3)$ in
@sec-csdr-embedding.
:::

The second constraint is a linear system for the scalars. The second example explains why its solutions are counted by
representation theory.

::: {#exm-constraints-scalars}
#### The scalar constraint

Constraint 2 is a linear system for the $\phi_a \in \mathfrak{g}$: $\phi$ intertwines the representation of $R$ on
$\mathfrak{k}$ with its representation on $\mathfrak{g}$ through $\tau$. By Schur's lemma (@sec-representations-schur)
its solutions are counted by matching irreducible representations (@def-csdr-rules); for the sphere the system
and its solution are in @sec-csdr-solution.
:::

Fermions are reduced by the same logic, with the spinor representation of the tangent space in place of the
representation on $\mathfrak{k}$. The third example states the result and the condition for chiral fermions.

::: {#exm-constraints-spinors}
#### Fermions

A spinor on $M_4 \times S/R$ in a representation $F$ of $G$ reduces to four-dimensional fermions in the
representations $h_i$ of $H$ for which $F \supset (r_i, h_i)$ and the spinor of $SO(\dim S/R)$ contains $r_i$
[@manolakos2016, eqs. 7-8]; chirality in four dimensions requires Weyl fermions in a higher dimension of the form
$4n + 2$, with the Majorana condition removing a doubling [@manolakos2016, p. 4].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise writes the scalar constraint out for the sphere. All it needs are the structure constants of
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$ in the basis $Q_a = \sigma_a/2i$.

::: {#exr-csd-constraint-sphere}
#### The constraints on the sphere

For $S = SU(2)$, $R = U(1)$ generated by $Q_3$ and $\mathfrak{k} = \operatorname{span}(Q_1, Q_2)$, with $[Q_a, Q_b] =
\epsilon_{abc}Q_c$, write constraints 2 and 3 explicitly for $\phi_1, \phi_2, \phi_3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[Q_3, Q_1] = Q_2$ and $[Q_3, Q_2] = -Q_1$, so $f_{31}{}^2 = 1$, $f_{32}{}^1 = -1$ and constraint 2 reads
$$
[\tau(Q_3), \phi_1] = \phi_2, \qquad [\tau(Q_3), \phi_2] = -\phi_1 ,
$$
while constraint 3 fixes $\phi_3 = \tau(Q_3)$. In words: $\operatorname{ad}\tau(Q_3)$ rotates the pair $(\phi_1, \phi_2)$ like a
vector in the tangent plane, exactly as $\operatorname{ad}Q_3$ rotates $(Q_1, Q_2)$. These are the equations solved in
@sec-csdr-solution.
:::

The second exercise takes the embedding to be trivial. It shows that the constraints then remove all scalars, and that
the remaining symmetric field is the pure four-dimensional gauge field with the full gauge group.

::: {#exr-csd-constraint-trivial}
#### The trivial embedding

Solve the constraints for the sphere with $\tau = 0$. Which gauge group and which scalars survive, and why is this the
case of strictly invariant fields?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\tau = 0$ constraint 1 is empty, so $A_\mu$ takes values in all of $\mathfrak{g}$; constraint 2 gives $0 = \phi_2$
and $0 = -\phi_1$, and constraint 3 gives $\phi_3 = 0$. No scalar survives, and the internal components of the field
vanish: $\hat A = A_\mu(x)dx^\mu$, invariant under rotations without any compensating transformation. This is the
content of @exm-symmetric-invariant: on the sphere the strictly invariant fields carry no internal components, and a
non-trivial embedding is needed for scalars.
:::

The third exercise checks that the constraints are compatible with the four-dimensional gauge symmetry. Without this
the reduced theory would not be a gauge theory with group $H$.

::: {#exr-csd-constraint-h-invariant}
#### The constraints are $H$-invariant

Show that if $(A_\mu, \phi_a)$ satisfies the constraints, so does its gauge transform by an $x$-dependent $h(x) \in H$:
$A_\mu \mapsto h^{-1}A_\mu h + h^{-1}\partial_\mu h$, $\phi_a \mapsto h^{-1}\phi_a h$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Elements of $H$ commute with every $\tau(Q_i)$. Then $[\tau(Q_i), h^{-1}\phi_a h] = h^{-1}[\tau(Q_i), \phi_a]h = f_{ia}{}^b
h^{-1}\phi_b h$, so constraint 2 is preserved; constraint 3 is preserved because $h^{-1}\tau(Q_i)h = \tau(Q_i)$; and
$h^{-1}A_\mu h$ and $h^{-1}\partial_\mu h \in \mathfrak{h}$ both commute with $\tau(\mathfrak{r})$, so constraint 1 is preserved.
The transformations of $G$ outside $H$ move $\tau$ and are not symmetries of the constrained system: the gauge group
in four dimensions is $H$.
:::
::::

### The rules

Solving the constraints case by case would be tedious. Representation theory turns the scalar constraint into a
matching problem between the decomposition of the adjoint of $G$ and the isotropy representation of the coset, and the
definition below states the resulting rules.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-csdr-rules}
#### CSDR rules

Decompose the adjoint of $G$ under $R \times H$ and the adjoint of $S$ under $R$,
$$
\operatorname{adj}G = (\operatorname{adj}R, 1) \oplus (1, \operatorname{adj}H) \oplus \sum_i(r_i, h_i), \qquad
\operatorname{adj}S = \operatorname{adj}R \oplus \sum_js_j ,
$$ {#eq-csdr-rules}
[@manolakos2016, eqs. 5-6]. Then: the four-dimensional gauge group is $H$; for every pair $r_i = s_j$ of identical
irreducible representations of $R$ there survives one scalar multiplet in the representation $h_i$ of $H$; all
other scalars vanish.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The rules are applied first to the running example. The charges of the adjoint of $SU(3)$ under the embedded $U(1)$ are
those of @fig-csdr-constraints, and the tangent space of the sphere has charges $\pm1$.

::: {#exm-rules-sphere}
#### The sphere with $G = SU(3)$

$\operatorname{adj}SU(2) = \operatorname{adj}U(1) \oplus (+1) \oplus (-1)$ and, for the embedding of
@sec-csdr-embedding, $\operatorname{adj}SU(3) = (0, \mathbf{3}) \oplus (0, \mathbf{1}) \oplus (+1, \mathbf{2}) \oplus
(-1, \mathbf{2})$ (@fig-csdr-constraints, @exr-csdr-branching): one complex doublet of $SU(2) \times U(1)$
survives, the Higgs field.
:::

The same sphere with the smaller gauge group $SU(2)$ is the example worked out in the review of Kubyshin and
collaborators. It shows that the normalisation of the embedding decides whether any scalar survives.

::: {#exm-rules-su2}
#### The sphere with $G = SU(2)$

With $\tau_n(Q_3) = nQ_3$, $\operatorname{adj}SU(2) = (0) \oplus (n) \oplus (-n)$ under $\tau_n(R)$: for $n = \pm1$ one
complex scalar $f$ survives, for $|n| \geq 2$ none, and the symmetric field is a pure monopole of charge $n$
[@kubyshin2003, eqs. 31-33] (@exr-csdr-su2-example).
:::

The rules are not limited to small groups. The third example quotes a model of current interest, in which the same
counting produces a grand unified group with a family of scalars and fermions.

::: {#exm-rules-e8}
#### A realistic case

$E_8$ over the nearly-Kähler coset $SU(3)/U(1) \times U(1)$ gives $H = E_6 \times U(1) \times U(1)$ with scalars and
fermions in the $\mathbf{27}$ of $E_6$, and a potential that breaks supersymmetry softly [@manolakos2016, eqs.
14-15]; the Wilson-flux mechanism then breaks $E_6$ further. The same rules, applied to a bigger group.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}

the adjoint of $H = SU(2) \times U(1)$, and two doublets of charges $\pm1$. Right: the tangent space of the sphere

embedded $U(1)$ and its electric charge $Q_{em} = T_3 + \tfrac12\tau$ of @sec-csdr-potential. The charge under the
embedded $U(1)$ is proportional to the vertical coordinate, so the rule reads off the doublet as the upper row.

$SU(2)$ under its $U(1)$, and apply the rule.

::: {#exr-csdr-su2-example}

The third exercise applies the rules to a larger gauge group with an embedding that has two blocks of equal entries. It
produces a different four-dimensional theory, with two $SU(2)$ factors and a scalar in a bi-doublet.

::: {#exr-csd-rules-su4}
#### $SU(4)$ on the sphere

For $G = SU(4)$ and $\tau(Q_3) = \tfrac{i}{2}\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -1, -1)$, find the charges of the adjoint under
$\tau$, the centraliser $H$ and the surviving scalars.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The charges of the matrix units are $t_i - t_j \in \{0, \pm1\}$: $15 \to 7 \cdot (0) + 4 \cdot (+1) + 4 \cdot (-1)$. The
charge-0 part is the block-diagonal algebra $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{u}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(2))$, so $H = S(U(2) \times U(2))$,
locally $SU(2) \times SU(2) \times U(1)$; the charge $+1$ part is the upper-right $2 \times 2$ block, on which the two
$SU(2)$ factors act from the left and from the right. One complex bi-doublet $(\mathbf{2}, \mathbf{2})$ survives, eight
real scalars: the structure of a left-right symmetric Higgs sector.

{{< sage exr-csd-rules-su4 >}}
:::
::::

The rules and the constraints are quoted, not derived, in this tutorial. The proposition below records them as cited
results; for the sphere, the rest of this chapter and the next derive everything they predict by explicit computation.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-csdr-rules-text}
#### Wang's theorem and the CSDR rules

The equivalence of the symmetric-field condition @eq-symmetric-field with the constraints of
@def-csdr-constraints, and the counting rules @eq-csdr-rules, are taken from @kubyshin2003 [Sec. 3, eqs.
17-24] and @manolakos2016 [Sec. 2]; for the sphere the constraints are written out and solved explicitly in
@sec-csdr-solution.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The counting in the rules is a statement about dimensions, which can be checked independently of the matching. The
first example does this for the running example.

::: {#exm-csd-rules-dimensions}
#### The dimension count

For $SU(3)$ the decomposition @eq-csdr-rules reads $8 = 4 + 2 + 2$ in complex dimensions (the abelian $R$ has no
summand of its own, because $\tau(Q_3)$ commutes with itself and lies in $\mathfrak{h}$), and the two matched pieces
$(\pm1, \mathbf{2})$ are conjugate to each other: one complex doublet, four real scalars, out of the sixteen of
@exr-csd-count-components.
:::

When no representation matches, the rules predict no scalars at all. The second example gives the simplest such case,
an abelian gauge group, where the surviving symmetric field is a pure monopole.

::: {#exm-csd-rules-abelian}
#### An abelian gauge group

For $G = U(1)$ the adjoint is the trivial representation, of charge $0$, which never matches the charges $\pm1$ of the
tangent space: no scalar survives, $H = U(1)$, and the symmetric field is $A(x) + \tau(\theta^3 Q_3)$, a
four-dimensional Maxwell field plus a fixed monopole on the sphere, with the monopole charge fixed by $\tau$.
:::

The third example explains why the reduced theory obtained from the rules is consistent. The underlying principle is
general and applies whenever a theory is restricted to the fields invariant under a compact symmetry group.

::: {#exm-csd-rules-criticality}
#### Symmetric criticality

The action is invariant under the isometries combined with gauge transformations, and the symmetric fields are the
fixed points of this action of $S$. By the principle of symmetric criticality, valid for compact $S$ [@kubyshin2003,
p. 12], a symmetric field that extremises the action among symmetric fields extremises it among all fields: the
four-dimensional equations of the reduced fields imply the higher-dimensional ones.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise turns @exm-csd-rules-criticality into an argument. It contrasts the symmetric fields with the
truncation of Part IV, where consistency failed.

::: {#exr-csdr-why-consistent}
#### Why symmetric fields avoid the consistency problem

Explain why the reduced equations of symmetric fields are exactly the restriction of the higher-dimensional
equations, in contrast with @def-consistency-problem.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The space of symmetric fields is invariant under the $S$-action, and the action functional is $S$-invariant;
by the principle of symmetric criticality [@kubyshin2003, p. 12] a critical point of the action restricted to
symmetric fields is a critical point of the full action. The higher-dimensional equations evaluated on a
symmetric field are $S$-covariant, so their $y$-dependence is a gauge transformation and they reduce to the
four-dimensional equations: no massive mode is sourced. In Part IV the ansatz was not closed under the isometries
with compensating gauge transformations, which is what allowed $K_a\cdot K_b$ to vary.
:::

The second exercise applies the rules to the abelian case of @exm-csd-rules-abelian with an arbitrary embedding. The
embedding of $U(1)$ in $U(1)$ is a single integer, and the integer turns out to be the monopole charge.

::: {#exr-csd-rules-u1}
#### $U(1)$ on the sphere

Let $G = U(1)$ and $\tau(Q_3) = \tfrac{i}{2}n$ (in the normalisation where $e^{4\pi Q_3} = 1$ in $SU(2)$). Solve the
constraints, and compute the flux $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{S^2} d\hat A$ of the internal field $\hat A = \tau(\theta^3 Q_3)/i$
with $\theta^3 = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ of @exr-csd-local-form-sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Constraint 2 reads $[\tau, \phi_1] = \phi_2$, $[\tau, \phi_2] = -\phi_1$, and all commutators vanish in an abelian algebra:
$\phi_1 = \phi_2 = 0$. Constraint 1 is empty and $H = U(1)$. The internal field is $\hat A = \tfrac{n}{2}\cos\theta\,d\varphi$
with $d\hat A = -\tfrac{n}{2}\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$, whose integral over the sphere is $-2\pi n$: the flux is $-n$,
an integer, the monopole charge of the symmetric field. That the embedding must be a homomorphism of groups, not only
of Lie algebras, is what makes $n$ an integer: Dirac's quantisation reappears as a condition on $\tau$.
:::

The third exercise is about the general structure of the counting. It derives the number of real scalars from the
rules for any $G$ on the sphere.

::: {#exr-csd-rules-general-count}
#### The number of scalars on the sphere

On $S^2 = SU(2)/U(1)$ the tangent space carries the charges $\pm1$. Show that the number of real scalars surviving the
constraints equals the complex dimension of the charge $+1$ eigenspace of $\operatorname{ad}\tau(Q_3)$ on
$\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb{C}}$ times two, and that the gauge group has dimension equal to that of the charge $0$ eigenspace.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @exr-csd-constraint-sphere, the complex combination $\phi_+ = \phi_1 - i\phi_2$ satisfies $[\tau, \phi_+] = i\phi_+$, so
it lies in the $+i$ eigenspace $\mathfrak{g}_{+i}$; conversely any $\phi_+ \in \mathfrak{g}_{+i}$ determines the real
fields through $\phi_- = -\phi_+^\dagger$ and $\phi_1 = (\phi_+ + \phi_-)/2$, $\phi_2 = \tfrac{i}{2}(\phi_+ - \phi_-)$. The
solution space is therefore $\mathfrak{g}_{+i}$ as a real vector space, of real dimension $2\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\mathfrak{g}_{+i}$.
The gauge algebra is the kernel of $\operatorname{ad}\tau$ in the real form $\mathfrak{g}$, whose real dimension equals
the complex dimension of the kernel in $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb{C}}$. For $SU(3)$: $2 \cdot 2 = 4$ scalars and a
four-dimensional $H$.
:::
::::

### Worked computations

The rules make a definite prediction for the running example, which can be checked by computing charges directly. The
proposition below records the result, which @fig-csdr-constraints displays.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-csd-sphere-matching}
#### The matching on the sphere

For $G = SU(3)$ and $\tau(Q_3) = \tfrac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$, the adjoint of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ has four
states of charge $0$ with $T_3$ weights $-1, 0, 0, 1$ (the adjoint of $SU(2) \times U(1)$), two states of charge $+1$
with $T_3 = \pm\tfrac12$ (a doublet) and two of charge $-1$; the tangent space of $S^2$ has the charges $\pm1$; the rule of
@def-csdr-rules leaves one complex doublet, four real scalars.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Checked by exact computation in `figures/csdr_constraints.sage`.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The charges can be read off from the root diagram of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$. The first example explains the geometry of
@fig-csdr-constraints.

::: {#exm-csd-matching-roots}
#### Charges from the root diagram

The six roots of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ form a regular hexagon in the $(T_3, Y_n)$ plane, and the charge under $\tau$ is
$2Y_n/\sqrt3$. The two roots on the horizontal axis ($E_{12}, E_{21}$) have charge $0$ and, with the two Cartan
generators, form the adjoint of $SU(2) \times U(1)$; the upper two roots ($E_{13}, E_{23}$) have charge $+1$, the lower two
charge $-1$. This is the branching @eq-branching-su3 of @sec-branching.
:::

The tangent space side of the rule is just as explicit. The second example recalls the charges of the isotropy
representation of the sphere.

::: {#exm-csd-matching-tangent}
#### Charges of the tangent space

$[Q_3, Q_1 \mp iQ_2] = \pm i(Q_1 \mp iQ_2)$: the complexified tangent space of the sphere at the pole has charges
$\pm1$ under the isotropy generator, the vector representation of $SO(2)$ (@exm-isotropy-sphere). Only the charge $+1$
states of $\mathfrak{g}$ can be matched with $Q_+ = Q_1 - iQ_2$.
:::

The proposition also contains a negative statement: nothing else matches. The third example lists the states that do not
survive and why.

::: {#exm-csd-matching-rest}
#### What does not survive

The charge-0 states would need a charge-0 direction in $\mathfrak{k}$, which does not exist ($Q_3$ belongs to $\mathfrak{r}$,
and its partner is constraint 3, $\phi_3 = \tau$); no state of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ has charge $\pm2$ or more, so even a
coset with such charges would add nothing. Of the sixteen real scalars only the doublet is left.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise recomputes the weights of @exm-csd-matching-roots in Sage. It checks the hexagon and the charge
classes at the same time.

::: {#exr-csd-matching-weights}
#### Weights and charges

Compute the weights $(T_3, Y_n)$ of the six root vectors $E_{ij}$ with $T_3 = \tfrac12\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 0)$ and
$Y_n = \operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)/2\sqrt3$, their charges $2Y_n/\sqrt3$, and group them by charge.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The weight of $E_{ij}$ is the difference of the $i$-th and $j$-th diagonal entries; all six have length $1$, and the
classes are those of @prp-csd-sphere-matching:

{{< sage exr-csd-matching-weights >}}
:::

The second exercise decomposes the fundamental representation in the same way. The result is needed whenever matter in
the $\mathbf{3}$ is added to the model.

::: {#exr-csd-matching-fundamental}
#### The fundamental representation

Decompose the $\mathbf{3}$ of $SU(3)$ under $SU(2) \times U(1)_\tau$ and give the charges under $\tau$ and under $Q_{em} =
T_3 + \tfrac12\tau$ (in units of $i$).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tau = \tfrac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$ acts on the basis vectors $e_1, e_2, e_3$ with charges $\tfrac13, \tfrac13, -
\tfrac23$; the $SU(2)$ block acts on $(e_1, e_2)$. So $\mathbf{3} \to (\mathbf{2}, \tfrac13) \oplus (\mathbf{1}, -\tfrac23)$.
The electric charges $T_3 + \tfrac12\tau$ are $\tfrac12 + \tfrac16 = \tfrac23$, $-\tfrac12 + \tfrac16 = -\tfrac13$ and $0 - \tfrac13 = -
\tfrac13$: the charges of the up and down quarks, a coincidence of the $\lambda_8$ embedding.
:::

The third exercise applies the fermion rule of @exm-constraints-spinors to all small representations of $SU(3)$. The
answer is that no fermion survives in this model, for a reason that can be read off from the charges.

::: {#exr-csd-matching-fermions}
#### No fermions

Fermions on $S^2$ couple to the spinor of $SO(2)$, of charges $\pm\tfrac12$ under the isotropy generator. Compute the
$\tau$-charges of the $\mathbf{3}, \bar{\mathbf{3}}, \mathbf{6}, \mathbf{8}, \mathbf{10}, \mathbf{15}, \mathbf{27}$ of $SU(3)$ and decide
which fermions survive.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
All charges are multiples of $\tfrac13$, because the entries of $\tau/i$ are, and $\pm\tfrac12$ is never a multiple of
$\tfrac13$: no representation $F$ contains a component matching the spinor, and no fermion survives. This is a known
limitation of the model, which is a reduction of pure Yang-Mills theory; realistic models need a different coset or
embedding (@exm-rules-e8).

{{< sage exr-csd-matching-fermions >}}
:::
::::

## The embedding of $U(1)$ in $SU(3)$ {#sec-csdr-embedding}

The data of a CSDR model are the coset, the gauge group and the embedding of the isotropy group in the gauge
group. For the running example the coset is $S^2 = SU(2)/U(1)$ (@exm-coset-sphere), the gauge group is $SU(3)$,
and the isotropy $U(1)$ is embedded along the hypercharge direction of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$. This section defines the
embedding, computes the eigenspaces of its adjoint action, and identifies the centraliser $H = SU(2) \times U(1)$,
with the matrix statements proved on explicit $3 \times 3$ matrices; this is the classic model of Manton [@manton1979;
@forgacs1980], reviewed in @kapetanakis1992. It has three subsections: the embedding itself, the eigenspaces of its
adjoint action together with the centraliser, and the propositions about them.

### The embedding

An embedding of a one-parameter group is fixed by the image of its generator. The definition below makes this choice
for the running example and explains why a diagonal generator is no loss of generality.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-csdr-embedding}
#### Embedding of $R$ in $G$

The **embedding** is a Lie algebra homomorphism $\tau: \mathfrak{r} \to \mathfrak{g}$ (@def-homomorphism); for $R = U(1)$
with generator $Q_3 = \sigma_3/2i$ it is the choice of one element $\tau(Q_3) \in \mathfrak{su}(3)$, which by conjugation
can be taken diagonal, $\tau(Q_3) = i\operatorname{diag}(t_1, t_2, t_3)$ with $\sum t_i = 0$. For the running example
$$
\tau(Q_3) = \frac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2) = \frac{i}{\sqrt3}\,\lambda_8 ,
$$ {#eq-csdr-tau}
the direction of the Gell-Mann matrix $\lambda_8$ (@eq-gell-mann), anti-Hermitian and traceless (@prp-csdr-embedding).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A diagonal generator acts on matrix units by multiplication with differences of its entries. The first example records
the resulting charges, which are all that is needed for the rest of the chapter.

::: {#exm-embedding-charges}
#### Charges of the matrix units

$[\tau(Q_3), E_{ij}] = i(t_i - t_j)E_{ij}$ for the matrix unit $E_{ij}$: with $t = (\tfrac13, \tfrac13, -\tfrac23)$ the
charges are $0$ on the $2 \times 2$ block and the corner, $+i$ on $E_{13}, E_{23}$ and $-i$ on $E_{31}, E_{32}$
(@fig-csdr-embedding, @exr-csdr-eigenspaces).
:::

The overall scale of $\tau$ is not free. The second example explains how the charges of the tangent space of the sphere
fix it.

::: {#exm-embedding-normalisation}
#### Why this normalisation

The tangent space of the sphere has charges $\pm i$ under $\operatorname{ad}Q_3$ (@exm-isotropy-sphere); the rule
of @def-csdr-rules needs equal charges in $\mathfrak{g}$, which fixes $t_1 - t_3 = 1$: a different multiple of
$\lambda_8$ would leave no scalars, as $\tau_n$ with $|n| \geq 2$ does for $SU(2)$ (@exm-rules-su2).
:::

Other directions in the Cartan subalgebra give other models. The third example shows that the $T_3$ direction gives a
smaller gauge group and a single singlet scalar.

::: {#exm-embedding-other}
#### Other embeddings

$\tau(Q_3) = \tfrac{i}{2}\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 0)$, the $T_3$ direction, has charges $\pm i$ on $E_{12}, E_{21}$ and
$\pm\tfrac{i}{2}$ on the other off-diagonal units: the centraliser is $U(1) \times U(1)$ and one complex singlet
survives, a different and less interesting model. The embedding is part of the data.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![The embedding $\tau = \tfrac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$ and the decomposition of $3 \times 3$ matrices under
$\operatorname{ad}\tau$: the block-diagonal kernel, the Lie algebra of the centraliser $H = SU(2) \times U(1)$; the
upper-right column, the $+i$ eigenspace, which carries the doublet $\varphi_+ = (\Phi_1, \Phi_2)$; and the lower-left
row, the $-i$ eigenspace of its conjugate. Sage checks the eigenvalues on the matrix units and the kernel.
Generated by `figures/csdr_embedding.sage`.](figures/csdr_embedding.svg){#fig-csdr-embedding width=70%}

The first exercise works out the alternative embedding of @exm-embedding-other in detail. It is the same computation as
for the running example, with a different diagonal.

::: {#exr-csdr-other-embedding}
#### The $T_3$ embedding

For $\tau(Q_3) = \tfrac{i}{2}\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 0)$ find the charges of all matrix units, the centraliser and the
surviving scalars.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$t = (\tfrac12, -\tfrac12, 0)$: the charges $t_i - t_j$ are $\pm1$ for $E_{12}, E_{21}$, and $\pm\tfrac12$ for $E_{13}, E_{31},
E_{23}, E_{32}$ ($+\tfrac12$ for $E_{13}$ and $E_{32}$, $-\tfrac12$ for $E_{31}$ and $E_{23}$). The kernel is the diagonal
algebra, so $H = U(1) \times U(1)$, generated by $T_3$ and $\lambda_8$. The $+i$ eigenspace is $\operatorname{span}(E_{12})$:
one complex scalar survives, charged under $T_3$ (charge $1$) and neutral under $\lambda_8$, the $SU(2)$ model of
@exm-rules-su2 embedded in the upper block of $SU(3)$. There is no doublet and no non-abelian factor: the hypercharge
embedding @eq-csdr-tau is what produces the electroweak structure.
:::

The second exercise looks at the embedding at the level of groups. The Lie algebra map is a homomorphism, but its
exponential reveals a subtlety of the global structure.

::: {#exr-csdr-tau-exponential}
#### The group element

Compute $\exp(\alpha\tau(Q_3))$ and check that it lies in $SU(3)$. For which $\alpha$ is it the identity, and how does
this compare with the period of $\exp(\alpha Q_3)$ in $SU(2)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\exp(\alpha\tau) = \operatorname{diag}(e^{i\alpha/3}, e^{i\alpha/3}, e^{-2i\alpha/3})$, unitary with determinant $1$; it is the
identity when $\alpha/3 \in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, so its period is $6\pi$. In $SU(2)$, $\exp(\alpha Q_3) = \operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\alpha/2},
e^{i\alpha/2})$ has period $4\pi$ (and $2\pi$ in $SO(3)$). The two periods do not agree: at $\alpha = 4\pi$, where
$\exp(\alpha Q_3) = 1$, one has $\exp(4\pi\tau) = e^{4\pi i/3}\,\mathbb{1}$, a non-trivial element of the centre $\mathbb{Z}_3$ of
$SU(3)$. So $\tau$ integrates to a group homomorphism from the isotropy $U(1)$ of $SU(2)$ only into $SU(3)/\mathbb{Z}_3$; on
the adjoint representation, where the centre acts trivially, this is all that is needed, and the constraints, being
infinitesimal, do not see the difference. For fields in the $\mathbf{3}$ it matters: their $\tau$-charges $\tfrac13, \tfrac13, -
\tfrac23$ are not half-integers, the charges allowed by the isotropy $U(1)$ of $SU(2)$, the same arithmetic that removes
the fermions in @exr-csd-matching-fermions.

{{< sage exr-csd-embedding-period >}}
:::

The third exercise asks which diagonal embeddings are equivalent. Conjugation by a permutation matrix reorders the
entries, so only the unordered triple of eigenvalues matters.

::: {#exr-csd-embedding-conjugate}
#### Equivalent embeddings

Show that two embeddings $\tau, \tau' \in \mathfrak{su}(3)$ conjugate by an element of $SU(3)$ give isomorphic reduced
theories, and that $\tfrac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$, $\tfrac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(1, -2, 1)$ and
$\tfrac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(-2, 1, 1)$ are conjugate. Is $-\tau$ conjugate to $\tau$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $\tau' = g\tau g^{-1}$, the map $X \mapsto gXg^{-1}$ is an automorphism of $\mathfrak{g}$ that carries the constraints for
$\tau$ into those for $\tau'$, the centraliser $H$ into $gHg^{-1}$ and the solutions into each other; the reduced
Lagrangians correspond. A permutation matrix (times a phase to make its determinant $1$) permutes the diagonal
entries, so the three matrices are conjugate. $-\tau$ has eigenvalues $\tfrac{i}{3}(-1, -1, 2)$, not a permutation of
$\tfrac{i}{3}(1, 1, -2)$, so it is not conjugate to $\tau$ in $SU(3)$; it gives the conjugate model, in which the surviving
scalar is the conjugate doublet in the row $(E_{31}, E_{32})$ (equivalently, after a permutation, the row
$(E_{12}, E_{13})$, @exr-csd-int-scan).
:::
::::

### Eigenspaces and the centraliser

The constraints involve $\operatorname{ad}\tau$, so its eigenspaces organise everything. The definition below lists them for
the running example; their dimensions add up to the dimension of $\mathfrak{gl}(3, \mathbb{C})$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-adjoint-eigenspaces}
#### Eigenspaces of $\operatorname{ad}\tau$

The **eigenspaces** of $\operatorname{ad}\tau(Q_3)$ on $\mathfrak{gl}(3, \mathbb{C})$ are
$$
\mathfrak{g}_0 = \{X : X_{13} = X_{23} = X_{31} = X_{32} = 0\}, \qquad
\mathfrak{g}_{+i} = \operatorname{span}(E_{13}, E_{23}), \qquad
\mathfrak{g}_{-i} = \operatorname{span}(E_{31}, E_{32}) ,
$$ {#eq-csdr-eigenspaces}
of dimensions $5 + 2 + 2 = 9$ over $\mathbb{C}$; intersected with $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ the kernel has real dimension
$4$ and the two eigenspaces together $4$, $4 + 4 = 8$ (@prp-csdr-eigenspaces).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The $+i$ eigenspace is where the scalars live. The first example describes it as a column vector on which the
centraliser acts.

::: {#exm-eigenspaces-doublet}
#### The doublet

$\mathfrak{g}_{+i}$ is the third column above the diagonal: a vector $(\Phi_1, \Phi_2)^T$ on which the $SU(2)$ block
acts by matrix multiplication, a **doublet**, and the $U(1)$ by a phase; this is where the scalar fields of
@sec-csdr-solution live.
:::

The two non-zero eigenspaces are not independent once the reality condition of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ is imposed. The second
example explains the pairing.

::: {#exm-eigenspaces-conjugate}
#### The conjugate

$\mathfrak{g}_{-i} = \mathfrak{g}_{+i}^\dagger$: anti-Hermiticity pairs the two eigenspaces, so the real solution of
the constraints has one complex doublet, not two.
:::

The eigenspace decomposition is a branching rule in disguise. The third example makes the connection with the
representation theory of @sec-branching.

::: {#exm-eigenspaces-branching}
#### The branching

@eq-csdr-eigenspaces is the branching $\mathbf{8} \to (\mathbf{3}, 0) \oplus (\mathbf{1}, 0) \oplus (\mathbf{2}, +1)
\oplus (\mathbf{2}, -1)$ of @sec-branching, the charges now those of the embedded $U(1)$ in the normalisation of
@eq-csdr-tau (@exr-csdr-branching).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes the eigenspaces by brute force. Sage solves the linear systems $[\tau, X] = \lambda X$ for a
general matrix $X$ and also solves the constraints directly.

::: {#exr-csdr-eigenspaces}
#### Eigenspaces in Sage

Solve $[\tau, X] = \lambda X$ for $\lambda = i, -i, 0$ over the $3 \times 3$ matrices and read off the spaces of
@eq-csdr-eigenspaces.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-csdr-eigenspaces >}}
:::

The second exercise shows that the eigenspace decomposition is compatible with the bracket. This grading is what makes
the commutator $[\phi_+, \phi_-]$ of the next chapter land in the gauge algebra.

::: {#exr-csd-eigen-grading}
#### A grading of the Lie algebra

Show that $[\mathfrak{g}_\lambda, \mathfrak{g}_\mu] \subseteq \mathfrak{g}_{\lambda + \mu}$ (with $\mathfrak{g}_{\pm2i} = 0$). Deduce that
$[\mathfrak{g}_{+i}, \mathfrak{g}_{+i}] = 0$, that $[\mathfrak{g}_{+i}, \mathfrak{g}_{-i}] \subseteq \mathfrak{g}_0$, and that
$\mathfrak{g}_0$ acts on $\mathfrak{g}_{+i}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{ad}\tau$ is a derivation: $[\tau, [X, Y]] = [[\tau, X], Y] + [X, [\tau, Y]] = (\lambda + \mu)[X, Y]$ for
$X \in \mathfrak{g}_\lambda$, $Y \in \mathfrak{g}_\mu$ (Jacobi identity). Since $\pm2i$ is not an eigenvalue, $[\mathfrak{g}_{+i},
\mathfrak{g}_{+i}] = 0$ (directly: $E_{13}E_{23} = E_{23}E_{13} = 0$); $[\mathfrak{g}_{+i}, \mathfrak{g}_{-i}] \subseteq \mathfrak{g}_0$,
for instance $[E_{13}, E_{31}] = E_{11} - E_{33}$; and $[\mathfrak{g}_0, \mathfrak{g}_{+i}] \subseteq \mathfrak{g}_{+i}$, which is the
statement that the centraliser acts on the scalars.
:::

The third exercise restricts the eigenspaces to the real form $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, where the fields actually live. It
explains the real dimensions quoted in the definition.

::: {#exr-csd-eigen-real}
#### Real dimensions

Show that $X \in \mathfrak{su}(3)$ decomposes as $X = X_0 + X_+ + X_-$ with $X_0 \in \mathfrak{g}_0 \cap \mathfrak{su}(3)$ and
$X_- = -X_+^\dagger$, and deduce the real dimensions $4$ (kernel) and $4$ (the two eigenspaces together).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Decompose $X$ into its block-diagonal part, its $(1,3), (2,3)$ entries and its $(3,1), (3,2)$ entries. Anti-Hermiticity
$X^\dagger = -X$ maps each block-diagonal entry to the conjugate of its mirror, so $X_0$ is anti-Hermitian and traceless,
an element of $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{u}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(1))$ of real dimension $3 + 1 = 4$; and it relates the column to
the row, $X_- = -X_+^\dagger$. The pair $(X_+, X_-)$ is determined by $X_+ \in \mathfrak{g}_{+i}$, two complex numbers, real
dimension $4$. Together $4 + 4 = 8 = \dim\mathfrak{su}(3)$, as checked in `csdr_embedding.sage`.
:::
::::

The kernel of $\operatorname{ad}\tau$ is a Lie algebra, and the group it generates is the four-dimensional gauge group.
The definition below names it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-csdr-centraliser}
#### The centraliser

The **centraliser** of the embedding is $H = C_G(\tau(R)) = \{g \in G : g\tau(Q_3)g^{-1} = \tau(Q_3)\}$, with Lie
algebra the kernel $\mathfrak{g}_0 \cap \mathfrak{su}(3)$ of $\operatorname{ad}\tau$. For @eq-csdr-tau it is the
block-diagonal subgroup $S(U(2) \times U(1)) \cong SU(2) \times U(1)$ of $SU(3)$: the four-dimensional gauge group of
the model is the electroweak group (@prp-csdr-eigenspaces).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A basis of the centraliser algebra exhibits its structure as a direct sum. The first example writes it down in terms
of Pauli matrices.

::: {#exm-centraliser-generators}
#### Its generators

$T_a = \tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ in the upper block ($a = 1, 2, 3$) and $\tau(Q_3)$ itself, the hypercharge: four
anti-Hermitian traceless matrices commuting with $\tau$, the $\mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(1)$ of
@exm-nonabelian-su2 with a $U(1)$ factor.
:::

The centraliser is defined for any embedding. The second example states the general fact and the dimension count it
implies.

::: {#exm-centraliser-general}
#### In general

$H$ is the subgroup of $G$ commuting with the image of $R$ [@manolakos2016, p. 3]; a larger $R$ gives a smaller
$H$, and the dimension counting $\dim\mathfrak{g} = \dim\mathfrak{h} + \sum\dim(r_i, h_i)$ of @eq-csdr-rules is
@prp-csdr-eigenspaces's $8 = 4 + 2 + 2$.
:::

For the smaller gauge group $SU(2)$ the centraliser is abelian. The third example gives it for all the embeddings
$\tau_n$.

::: {#exm-centraliser-kubyshin}
#### $SU(2)$ with $\tau_n$

For $G = SU(2)$ and $\tau_n(Q_3) = nQ_3$ the centraliser is the $U(1)$ generated by $Q_3$ itself, for every
$n \neq 0$: a $U(1)$ gauge theory with, for $n = \pm1$, one charged scalar [@kubyshin2003, Sec. 4].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes the centraliser as a real linear system on the Gell-Mann coordinates. It also checks that
the four generators close into $\mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(1)$.

::: {#exr-csd-centraliser-sage}
#### The centraliser in Sage

Write a general $X = \sum_k x_k\,i\lambda_k \in \mathfrak{su}(3)$, solve $[\tau, X] = 0$ for the real $x_k$, and check the
brackets of the solutions.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The kernel is spanned by $i\lambda_1, i\lambda_2, i\lambda_3, i\lambda_8$; the first three close into $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and the
fourth commutes with them:

{{< sage exr-csd-centraliser-sage >}}
:::

The second exercise identifies the global structure of the centraliser. As a group it is $U(2)$, which is locally, but not
globally, a product.

::: {#exr-csd-centraliser-u2}
#### The group $S(U(2) \times U(1))$

Show that $A \mapsto \operatorname{diag}(A, (\det A)^{-1})$ is an isomorphism $U(2) \to S(U(2) \times U(1))$, and that
$SU(2) \times U(1) \to U(2)$, $(B, e^{i\alpha}) \mapsto e^{i\alpha}B$, is surjective with kernel $\mathbb{Z}_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
An element of $S(U(2) \times U(1))$ is $\operatorname{diag}(A, u)$ with $A \in U(2)$, $|u| = 1$ and $u\det A = 1$, so $u$ is
determined by $A$; the map is a bijective homomorphism. Every $A \in U(2)$ is $e^{i\alpha}B$ with $e^{2i\alpha} = \det A$ and
$B = e^{-i\alpha}A \in SU(2)$, and $e^{i\alpha}B = 1$ forces $B = e^{-i\alpha}\mathbb{1}$ with $e^{-2i\alpha} = 1$, i.e.
$(B, e^{i\alpha}) = \pm(\mathbb{1}, 1)$. So $H \cong U(2) \cong (SU(2) \times U(1))/\mathbb{Z}_2$, which has the same Lie algebra as
$SU(2) \times U(1)$: the electroweak group of the Standard Model is also $U(2)$ in this sense.
:::

The third exercise surveys the possible centralisers of a diagonal embedding. The answer depends only on which entries
of $\tau$ coincide.

::: {#exr-csd-centraliser-types}
#### Which centralisers occur

For $\tau = i\operatorname{diag}(t_1, t_2, t_3) \neq 0$ with $\sum t_i = 0$, show that the centraliser is $U(1) \times U(1)$ if
the $t_i$ are distinct and $S(U(2) \times U(1))$ if two of them coincide. Can all three coincide?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[\tau, E_{ij}] = i(t_i - t_j)E_{ij}$, so the complexified kernel is spanned by the diagonal units and by those $E_{ij}$ with
$t_i = t_j$. With distinct entries it is the diagonal algebra, whose real form is the maximal torus $U(1) \times U(1)$;
with $t_1 = t_2 \neq t_3$ it adds $E_{12}, E_{21}$ and becomes the block-diagonal algebra of $S(U(2) \times U(1))$. All three
equal and summing to zero means $\tau = 0$, the trivial embedding of @exr-csd-constraint-trivial, with centraliser all of
$SU(3)$.
:::
::::

### Worked computations

The statements of this section are finite computations with $3 \times 3$ matrices, each reducing to finitely many
entries. The
first proposition records that $\tau$ is an element of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ and the charges of the matrix units that carry
the scalars.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-csdr-embedding}
#### The embedding

$\tau(Q_3) = \tfrac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$ is anti-Hermitian and traceless, and $[\tau, E_{13}] = iE_{13}$,
$[\tau, E_{23}] = iE_{23}$, $[\tau, E_{31}] = -iE_{31}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.CSDR.τ_mem_su3`, `KaluzaKlein.CSDR.ad_τ_E13`, `KaluzaKlein.CSDR.ad_τ_E23` and
`KaluzaKlein.CSDR.ad_τ_E31`.

**Sage.** Checked in `figures/csdr_embedding.sage`.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Matrix units can be labelled with indices starting at $1$ or at $0$. The first example translates between the two
conventions and gives the entrywise form of the bracket with $\tau$.

::: {#exm-csd-embedding-indices}
#### Matrix units and indices

With indices in $\{0, 1, 2\}$ the matrix unit $E_{jk}$ of the text is $E_{j-1,k-1}$, so $E_{13}$, $E_{23}$ and $E_{31}$
become $E_{02}$, $E_{12}$ and $E_{20}$. In either labelling $\tau = \operatorname{diag}(t_1, t_2, t_3)$ with $t_1 = t_2 = \tfrac{i}{3}$,
$t_3 = -\tfrac{2i}{3}$, and the bracket $[\tau, X] = \tau X - X\tau$ has the entries $(t_j - t_k)X_{jk}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** In `KaluzaKlein/CSDR/Embedding.lean` the matrix unit `E i j` has indices in `Fin 3 = {0, 1, 2}`, so `E 0 2` is
$E_{13}$, `E 1 2` is $E_{23}$ and `E 2 0` is $E_{31}$; `τ` is `diagonal ![I/3, I/3, -2*I/3]`, and the bracket `⁅τ, X⁆`
is the commutator $\tau X - X\tau$.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The bracket with a diagonal matrix is a one-line computation. The second example carries it out for $E_{13}$ and for
one unit of the kernel.

::: {#exm-csd-embedding-by-hand}
#### One bracket by hand

$\tau E_{13} = \tfrac{i}{3}E_{13}$ (the first diagonal entry multiplies the first row) and $E_{13}\tau = -\tfrac{2i}{3}E_{13}$
(the third diagonal entry multiplies the third column), so $[\tau, E_{13}] = (\tfrac{i}{3} + \tfrac{2i}{3})E_{13} = iE_{13}$.
The same computation gives $[\tau, E_{12}] = (\tfrac{i}{3} - \tfrac{i}{3})E_{12} = 0$.
:::

The proposition fixes the normalisation of $\tau$ relative to the other generators. The third example compares its
norm with that of $T_3$, a number that will set the Weinberg angle in the next chapter.

::: {#exm-csd-embedding-norm}
#### The norm of $\tau$

$\operatorname{Tr}\tau^2 = -\tfrac19(1 + 1 + 4) = -\tfrac23$, while $T_3 = \tfrac{i}{2}\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 0)$ has
$\operatorname{Tr}T_3^2 = -\tfrac12$. So $\tau$ is $\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$ times the generator $\tfrac{i}{2}\lambda_8$ normalised like
$T_3$, and the charge $1$ of the doublet under $\tau$ becomes $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ under the normalised generator.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes the whole matrix of $\operatorname{ad}\tau$ in the Gell-Mann basis. It confirms the eigenvalues
and the normalisation of @exm-csd-embedding-norm.

::: {#exr-csd-embedding-gellmann}
#### $\operatorname{ad}\tau$ on the Gell-Mann basis

Compute the $8 \times 8$ matrix of $\operatorname{ad}\tau$ in the basis $i\lambda_1, \dots, i\lambda_8$ of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, its
eigenvalues, and $\operatorname{Tr}\tau^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{ad}\tau$ vanishes on $i\lambda_1, i\lambda_2, i\lambda_3, i\lambda_8$ and acts as a rotation on each of the planes
$(i\lambda_4, i\lambda_5)$ and $(i\lambda_6, i\lambda_7)$; its eigenvalues are $0$ four times and $\pm i$ twice each:

{{< sage exr-csd-embedding-gellmann >}}
:::

The second exercise derives the brackets that the proposition does not list. Hermitian conjugation does most of the
work, and the rest follows from the charges of @exm-embedding-charges.

::: {#exr-csd-embedding-e32}
#### The remaining brackets

From $[\tau, E_{23}] = iE_{23}$ and $\tau^\dagger = -\tau$ deduce $[\tau, E_{32}] = -iE_{32}$, and compute $[\tau, E_{12}]$,
$[\tau, E_{21}]$ and $[\tau, E_{kk}]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Taking the adjoint of $\tau E_{23} - E_{23}\tau = iE_{23}$ gives $E_{32}\tau^\dagger - \tau^\dagger E_{32} = -iE_{32}$, and with
$\tau^\dagger = -\tau$ this is $\tau E_{32} - E_{32}\tau = -iE_{32}$. The units $E_{12}, E_{21}$ have charge $t_1 - t_2 = 0$ and
the diagonal units commute with the diagonal $\tau$: all of them lie in the kernel, the algebra of $H$.
:::

The third exercise asks for an independent hand check of anti-Hermiticity and tracelessness. These two properties are
what make $\tau$ a legitimate generator of $SU(3)$.

::: {#exr-csd-embedding-su3}
#### $\tau$ is in $\mathfrak{su}(3)$

Check $\tau^\dagger = -\tau$ and $\operatorname{Tr}\tau = 0$, and show that every diagonal anti-Hermitian traceless matrix is
a real combination of $iT_3$-type and $i\lambda_8$-type matrices. Which combination is $\tau$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tau^\dagger = -\tfrac{i}{3}\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2) = -\tau$ because the entries are imaginary, and the trace is
$\tfrac{i}{3}(1 + 1 - 2) = 0$. A diagonal anti-Hermitian traceless matrix is $i\operatorname{diag}(a, b, -a - b)$ with $a, b$
real, which equals $i\tfrac{a - b}{2}\lambda_3 + i\tfrac{\sqrt3(a + b)}{2}\lambda_8$ (compare the entries: $\lambda_3 =
\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 0)$, $\lambda_8 = \operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)/\sqrt3$). For $\tau$, $a = b = \tfrac13$: the $\lambda_3$
component vanishes and the $\lambda_8$ coefficient is $\tfrac{i}{\sqrt3}$, as in @eq-csdr-tau.
:::
::::

The second proposition upgrades the charges of individual matrix units to a description of the full eigenspaces. It
is the statement used to solve the constraints in the next chapter.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-csdr-eigenspaces}
#### Eigenspaces and centraliser

For every $3 \times 3$ complex matrix $X$: $[\tau, X] = iX$ if and only if all entries of $X$ other than $X_{13}, X_{23}$
vanish, and $[\tau, X] = 0$ if and only if $X_{13} = X_{23} = X_{31} = X_{32} = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.CSDR.eigenspace_plus_i` and `KaluzaKlein.CSDR.centraliser`, with the dimension count
`KaluzaKlein.CSDR.branching_dimensions`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.CSDR.eigenspace_plus_i >}}

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.CSDR.centraliser >}}

**Sage.** Checked in @exr-csdr-eigenspaces and `figures/csdr_embedding.sage`.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The proposition is an "if and only if" for all matrices, not only for the matrix units. The first example shows how the
entrywise form of the commutator gives both directions at once.

::: {#exm-csd-eigen-entrywise}
#### The entrywise form

For a diagonal $\tau = i\operatorname{diag}(t_1, t_2, t_3)$, $([\tau, X])_{jk} = i(t_j - t_k)X_{jk}$. The equation $[\tau, X] = iX$
is therefore the nine scalar equations $(t_j - t_k - 1)X_{jk} = 0$, and $X_{jk}$ is free exactly when $t_j - t_k = 1$, i.e.
for $(j, k) = (1, 3), (2, 3)$; otherwise it must vanish.
:::

A sample matrix illustrates the decomposition. The second example splits a simple integer matrix into its three
components and applies $\operatorname{ad}\tau$ to each.

::: {#exm-csd-eigen-sample}
#### A sample decomposition

$X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 & 9 \end{pmatrix}$ splits as the block-diagonal part with entries $1, 2, 4, 5, 9$
(in $\mathfrak{g}_0$), the column $3E_{13} + 6E_{23}$ (in $\mathfrak{g}_{+i}$) and the row $7E_{31} + 8E_{32}$ (in $\mathfrak{g}_{-i}$);
$[\tau, X] = i(3E_{13} + 6E_{23}) - i(7E_{31} + 8E_{32})$.
:::

The dimension count is the simplest consequence. The third example states it in the form used by the
rules of the previous section.

::: {#exm-csd-eigen-count}
#### The dimension count

The kernel of $\operatorname{ad}\tau$ in $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ is four-dimensional, and the $\pm i$ eigenspaces contribute $2 + 2$
real dimensions to $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ (one complex doublet): $4 + 2 + 2 = 8$, the content of @prp-csd-sphere-matching.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.CSDR.branching_dimensions`.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise decomposes a random matrix numerically exactly, using spectral projectors. It checks the
proposition on an example that is not built from matrix units.

::: {#exr-csd-eigen-generic-check}
#### Spectral projectors

With $P_\lambda = \prod_{\mu \neq \lambda}(\operatorname{ad}\tau - \mu)/(\lambda - \mu)$, $\lambda, \mu \in \{0, i, -i\}$, decompose a random
integer matrix into eigencomponents in Sage and compare with the proposition.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Since $\operatorname{ad}\tau(\operatorname{ad}\tau - i)(\operatorname{ad}\tau + i) = 0$ on $\mathfrak{gl}(3, \mathbb{C})$, the projectors are
well defined and sum to the identity; the components are exactly the block-diagonal part, the column and the row:

{{< sage exr-csd-eigen-generic-check >}}
:::

The second exercise derives the $-i$ eigenspace from the $+i$ one. The argument is the same conjugation as in
@exr-csd-embedding-e32, applied to a general matrix.

::: {#exr-csd-eigen-minus}
#### The $-i$ eigenspace

Using the proposition and $\tau^\dagger = -\tau$, show that $[\tau, X] = -iX$ holds exactly for the $X$ supported on the
entries $(3, 1), (3, 2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[\tau, X] = -iX$ is equivalent, after taking adjoints, to $[X^\dagger, \tau^\dagger] = iX^\dagger$, i.e. $[\tau, X^\dagger] = iX^\dagger$.
By the proposition $X^\dagger$ is supported on $(1, 3), (2, 3)$, so $X$ is supported on $(3, 1), (3, 2)$; the converse is the
same computation backwards.
:::

The third exercise proves that $\operatorname{ad}\tau$ is diagonalisable. This justifies speaking of eigenspaces that add
up to the whole algebra.

::: {#exr-csd-eigen-projectors}
#### $\operatorname{ad}\tau$ is diagonalisable

Show that $\operatorname{ad}\tau$ satisfies $p(\operatorname{ad}\tau) = 0$ with $p(z) = z(z - i)(z + i)$, and conclude that
$\mathfrak{gl}(3, \mathbb{C}) = \mathfrak{g}_0 \oplus \mathfrak{g}_{+i} \oplus \mathfrak{g}_{-i}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On the basis of matrix units $\operatorname{ad}\tau$ is diagonal with eigenvalues $i(t_j - t_k) \in \{0, i, -i\}$, so $p(\operatorname{ad}
\tau)$ vanishes on each $E_{jk}$ and hence everywhere. A linear map annihilated by a polynomial with distinct roots is
diagonalisable, and the space is the direct sum of its eigenspaces; the projectors are the Lagrange interpolation
polynomials of @exr-csd-eigen-generic-check.
:::
::::

## Exercises {#sec-01-symmetric-fields-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Three exercises that combine the two sections: a scan over all diagonal embeddings of $U(1)$ in $SU(3)$ with the rules
applied to each, the general block embedding in $SU(n)$, and a complete table for the $SU(2)$ model of Kubyshin and
collaborators.

The running example used one particular embedding. The first integrative exercise asks which other diagonal embeddings
leave scalars on the sphere, and what four-dimensional theory each produces.

::: {#exr-csd-int-scan}
#### All diagonal embeddings

Scan $\tau = i\operatorname{diag}(t_1, t_2, t_3)$ with $t_i \in \tfrac16\mathbb{Z}$, $\sum t_i = 0$ and $|t_i - t_j| \leq 2$, up to
permutations. For each embedding with scalars on $S^2$ give $\dim H$ and the charge $+1$ matrix units, and identify the
models with a doublet.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @exr-csd-rules-general-count the scalars are the matrix units with $t_i - t_j = 1$, and by @exr-csd-centraliser-types
$\dim H = 4$ exactly when two entries coincide. Six embeddings on the grid leave scalars. Only $\tfrac13(1, 1, -2)$ and its
negative (up to order) $\tfrac13(2, -1, -1)$ have a non-abelian $H = U(2)$ and a doublet; the others, such as
$\tfrac12(1, 0, -1)$ or $(1, 0, -1)$, have $H = U(1) \times U(1)$ and one or two charged singlets. The electroweak structure
is special to the $\lambda_8$ direction:

{{< sage exr-csd-int-scan >}}
:::

The block structure of the running example generalises to any $SU(n)$. The second integrative exercise works out the
general case and checks the dimension count of the rules.

::: {#exr-csd-int-sun}
#### Block embeddings in $SU(n)$

Let $G = SU(n)$ and $\tau = i\operatorname{diag}(a\mathbb{1}_k, (a - 1)\mathbb{1}_{n-k})$ with $a = (n - k)/n$. Show that $\tau$ is
traceless, find $H$ and the surviving scalars, and check $n^2 - 1 = \dim H + 2 \cdot 2k(n - k)$ in real dimensions.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{Tr}\tau = i(ka + (n - k)(a - 1)) = i(na - (n - k)) = 0$. The charges $t_i - t_j$ are $0$ within each block and
$\pm1$ between the blocks, so $H = S(U(k) \times U(n - k))$, of dimension $k^2 + (n - k)^2 - 1$, and the scalar is the
upper-right $k \times (n - k)$ block, a complex bifundamental $(\mathbf{k}, \overline{\mathbf{n - k}})$ with $2k(n - k)$ real
components. The off-diagonal blocks together have $2k(n - k)$ complex entries, i.e. real dimension $2k(n - k)$ inside
$\mathfrak{su}(n)$, and $k^2 + (n - k)^2 - 1 + 2k(n - k) = n^2 - 1$. For $n = 3$, $k = 2$ this is the running example
($a = \tfrac13$); for $n = 4$, $k = 2$ it is @exr-csd-rules-su4.
:::

The $SU(2)$ model is small enough to be described completely. The third integrative exercise collects its features for
the first few embeddings, including the monopole charge and the fate of fermions.

::: {#exr-csd-int-su2-table}
#### The $SU(2)$ model in a table

For $G = SU(2)$ on $S^2$ and $\tau_n(Q_3) = nQ_3$, $n = 0, 1, 2, 3$, give $H$, the number of real scalars, and whether
doublet fermions (charges $\pm\tfrac{n}{2}$ under $\tau_n$) can match the spinor charges $\pm\tfrac12$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$n = 0$: $H = SU(2)$, no scalar (@exr-csd-constraint-trivial), and doublet fermions have charge $0$, no match. $n = 1$:
$H = U(1)$, one complex scalar, two real (@exm-rules-su2), and the doublet has charges $\pm\tfrac12$, which match: one
four-dimensional fermion survives, the zero mode of the Dirac operator in the monopole background. $n = 2$: $H = U(1)$,
no scalar, the adjoint has charges $0, \pm2$ (no match), the doublet $\pm1$ (no match): a pure monopole of charge $2$.
$n = 3$: $H = U(1)$, no scalar, doublet charges $\pm\tfrac32$, no match. Only $n = 1$ gives a Higgs-type theory, the
abelian Higgs model of @exr-csdr-su2-example, with potential $\tfrac12(|f|^2 - 1)^2$.
:::
::::
